note: Only where the format (formats.json: the kind of online space) says something about an approach, whatever the community type (e.g. a team is a set group, not open to join, whatever kind of group it is). Marks from −2 (strongly against) to +2 (strongly for), each with a reason. Drafted 2026-10-10 after the held-out check (TODO.md, "Tuning"); reviewed by Sohyeon 2026-10-10 (peer production × open access raised to +2; citizen science × hierarchical decision-making dropped: it depends on who runs the project). items.why: People join by contributing: an edit, a patch, a translation.
Contributions are often matched to skills (code, writing, design).
Newcomers are often onboarded by experienced contributors.
Anyone can start contributing; that openness is how peer production works.
Whoever does the work usually decides how it is done.
Proposals usually go ahead unless someone objects.
Decisions often happen on the shared tools themselves (talk pages, issues, pull requests).
A team is a set group: people are hired, assigned or invited, not let in freely.
Team members are usually added by invitation.
Teams rarely choose members by lot.
Mailing lists often decide by lazy consensus: a proposal goes ahead if nobody objects in time.
Email is a poor fit for votes that stay open and keep changing.
Forums often give new members limited rights until they have taken part for a while (trust levels).
Forums often have levels of membership, with more rights as people take part.
Chat groups are often joined through an invite link.
